respStmt.resp: traduction anglaise depuis le grec (zoo71/1g), verification humaine requise

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo71/1g.xml (recension la plus ancienne et la plus exegetique du Physiologus grec, riche en citations scripturaires), lui-meme deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Chapitres correspondant au decoupage du temoin grec (memes xml:id) ; les numerotations doublees ou fractionnaires du temoin grec (10.1/10.2, 13.1/13.2, 28.1/28.2, 30.1/30.2, 31a/31b, 32.1/32.2, le doublon "33.1" applique a deux chapitres distincts sur l'hirondelle, 35 en trois parties, 37.1/37.2, 44 en trois parties) sont conservees telles quelles, sans renumerotation, pour rester fideles a la source ; des suffixes de desambiguisation ("a"/"b"/"2"/"3") ont ete ajoutes uniquement aux xml:id internes a cette traduction lorsque le temoin grec reutilisait le meme identifiant.

div.head: Concerning the Lion
div.p: We shall begin to speak concerning the lion, the king of the beasts [that is, of the animals].
For Jacob, blessing Judah, said: "Judah is a lion's whelp; from the shoot, my son, thou art gone up"; and so forth.
The Physiologus spoke concerning the lion, that it has three natures.

Its first nature is this: when it walks in the mountain and the scent of the hunters comes to it, with its tail it covers its own tracks, that the hunters, following its tracks, may not find its lair and seize it.

So too our Christ, the spiritual lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, sent from the unseen Father, covered his spiritual tracks, that is, his Godhead. Among angels he became an angel, among archangels an archangel, among thrones a throne, among powers a power, all the way down to his descent; and he came into the womb of the holy virgin Mary, that he might save the erring race of men, "and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." For this reason, not knowing him, those who had come down from above said, "Who is this King of glory?" Then the Holy Spirit says, "The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory."
The second nature of the lion: when the lion sleeps in its cave, its eyes stay wakeful, for they are open.

And in the Song of Songs Solomon bears witness, saying, "I sleep, but my heart waketh." So too the body of my Lord sleeps upon the cross, while his Godhead keeps watch at the right hand of God the Father; "for he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep."
The third nature of the lion: when the lioness bears her cub, she bears it dead, and watches over her offspring until the father, coming on the third day, breathes into its face, and raises it up.

So too our God the Almighty, the Father of all, on the third day raised up his first-born Son, who is before all creation, our Lord Jesus Christ, from the dead, that he might save the erring race of men. Well then did Jacob say: "he lay down and slept as a lion, and as a lion's whelp; who shall rouse him up?"

div.head: Concerning the Sun-Lizard
div.p: There is a lizard called the sun-lizard, as the Physiologus says. When it grows old, its eyes are hindered and it becomes blind, not seeing the light of the sun. What then does its own good nature do? It seeks a wall facing the sunrise, and enters into the crack of that wall [facing the sunrise]; and as the sun rises, its eyes are opened, and become sound again.

In this same manner, O man, if you wear the garment of the old man, and the eyes of your heart are grown dim, seek the rising sun of righteousness, Christ our God [whose name is called "the Dayspring" by the prophet], and he himself will open the eyes of your heart.

div.head: Concerning the Charadrius
div.p: There is a bird called the charadrius, as it is written in Deuteronomy. The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that this bird is wholly white, having no blackness at all in it, and its inward excrement heals eyes grown dim; and it is found in the courts of kings. If any man is sick, it is known from the charadrius whether he lives or dies; for they bring it before the sick man's bed, and if the man's sickness is unto death, the charadrius turns its face away from the sick man, and everyone knows that he will die; but if the man's sickness is unto life, the charadrius gazes fixedly at the sick man and the sick man at the charadrius, and the charadrius swallows down the sickness of the sick man, and flies up into the ether of the sun, and burns up the sickness of the sick man, and scatters it, and both the charadrius and the sick man are saved together.

It is good, then, to take this as a figure of the Saviour; for our Lord is wholly white, having no blackness at all, for he said, "the prince of this world cometh, and findeth nothing in me." For when the Lord came from the heavens to the Jews, he turned his Godhead away from them; but coming to us the Gentiles, and taking up our infirmities and bearing our sicknesses, he was lifted up upon the wood of the cross, and blotted out all our infirmities and sins; for having ascended on high, he led captivity captive. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the charadrius. But you will say to me that the charadrius is unclean according to the Law, and how then is it applied to the person of the Saviour? The serpent too is unclean, and yet John bore witness, saying, "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up." For creatures are twofold, some worthy of praise, some of blame.

div.head: Concerning the Pelican
div.p: Well does David say, "I am become like a pelican of the wilderness." The Physiologus spoke concerning the pelican, that it is exceedingly fond of its offspring; when it has borne its chicks and they have grown a little, they strike their parents in the face; and the parents, buffeting the chicks, kill them. But afterwards their parents are moved with compassion, and mourn for three days over the chicks which they killed. On the third day, then, their mother tears open her own sides, and her blood, dripping upon the dead bodies of the chicks, raises them to life.

So too the Lord said in Isaiah, "I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me." The maker of all creation begot us, and we struck him; how then did we strike him? We worshipped the creation rather than the Creator. Our Saviour, then, having ascended to the height of the cross and opened his own side, dripped forth blood and water for salvation and eternal life: the blood, for the sake of him who said, "taking the cup, he blessed it"; the water, for the baptism of repentance. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the pelican.

div.head: Concerning the Night-Raven
div.p: The Psalmist says: "I am become like a night-raven in a ruined house."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the night-raven, that this bird loves the night above the day.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ loved us who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, the people of the Gentiles, above the people of the Jews, who had inherited both the adoption and the promise of the fathers. For this reason the Saviour also said, "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom," and so forth. But you will say to me that the night-raven is unclean according to the Law, and how then is it applied to the person of the Saviour? Well said; but how does the Apostle say, "him who knew no sin, he made to be sin for us"? He humbled himself, that he might save all, and that we might be exalted. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the night-raven.

div.head: Concerning the Eagle
div.p: David says: "thy youth shall be renewed as the eagle's."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the eagle, that when it grows old, its eyes and its wings grow heavy and it becomes dim of sight. What then does it do? It seeks out a clear spring of water, and flies up into the ether of the sun, and burns off its own old wings and the dimness of its eyes, and comes down to the spring, and is baptized three times, and is renewed, and becomes young.

In this same manner, O man, if you wear the garment of the old man and the eyes of your heart are grown dim, seek the spiritual spring, the Word of God, who says, "they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water"; and fly up to the height of the sun of righteousness, Jesus Christ, and strip off the old man together with his deeds, and be baptized three times in the ever-flowing spring, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; and strip off the old man, that is, the old garment of the devil, and put on the new man, created according to God, and there shall be fulfilled also in you the prophecy of David: "thy youth shall be renewed as the eagle's."

div.head: Concerning the Bird Phoenix
div.p: The Lord said in the Gospel: "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again"; and the Jews were indignant at this saying.

There is a bird in India called the phoenix. Every five hundred years it enters into the woods of Lebanon, and fills its wings with spices, and gives a sign to the priest of Heliopolis in the new month, Nisan or Adar, that is, Phamenoth or Pharmuthi. And the priest, being given the sign, comes, and fills the altar with vine-wood; and the bird enters Heliopolis, laden with spices, and mounts the altar, and itself kindles the fire and burns itself up. On the next day the priest, searching the altar, finds a worm in the ashes; on the second day he finds it a fledgling bird; and on the third day he finds it a full-grown bird, and it greets the priest, and goes off to its own place.

If then this bird has power to kill itself and bring itself to life, how do the foolish Jews grow indignant against the Lord who said, "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again"? The phoenix, then, takes on the person of our Saviour; for coming from the heavens, and spreading out his two wings, he brought fragrance in fullness, that is, virtuous heavenly words, that we too, through our prayers, might stretch out our hands, and send up a spiritual fragrance through good ways of life. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the phoenix.

div.head: Concerning the Bird Hoopoe
div.p: It is written: "he who reviles father or mother, let him die the death." And how then are there some who are slayers of father and slayers of mother?

There is a bird called the hoopoe. Its young, if they see their parents grown old, pluck out their parents' old feathers, and lick their eyes, and warm their parents beneath their own wings, and make them fledglings again, and they become young once more, the young saying to their parents: just as you made us fledglings and toiled, labouring and feeding us, so shall we do the same for you.
How then do foolish men not love their own parents, [who raised them and instructed them in the admonition of the Lord]? Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the hoopoe.

div.head: Concerning the Wild Ass
div.p: It is written in Job: "who let the wild ass go free?"
The Physiologus spoke concerning the wild ass, that it is the leader of the herd, and if the females bear males, their father cuts off all their genitals entirely, that they may not sow seed.

The patriarchs sought to sow bodily seed, but the apostles, seeking spiritual children, practised continence, asking for a heavenly seed, as it is written: "Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not, for more are the children of the desolate than of her that hath a husband." The old covenant is the seed of promise, but the new is of continence. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the wild ass.

div.head: Concerning the Viper
div.p: Well did John say to the Pharisees: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?"

The Physiologus spoke concerning the viper, that the male has the face of a man, but the female the face of a woman; down to the navel they have the shape of a human, but they have the tail of a crocodile. The female has no passage in her womb, but only as it were the eye of a needle. If the male mates with the female, he ejects his seed into the female's mouth, and if the female swallows the seed, she bites off the male's necessary parts, and the male dies at once. And as the young grow, they eat through their mother's belly, and so come forth; they are therefore slayers of both father and mother.

Well then did John liken the Pharisees to the viper; for in the manner that the viper kills its father and its mother, so too these men killed their own spiritual fathers, the prophets, he says, and our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Church. How then shall they flee from the wrath to come? For the father and the mother live for ever, but these men have died.

div.head: Concerning the Viper (continued)
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning the viper: when the male first unites with the female, he unites with her mouth, and the female, swallowing his seed, bites off his necessary parts; he knows, then, that if he unites with the female, he will die. Many times, then, he goes and comes to the female, and at once turns away from her; but afterwards, unable to restrain himself, he unites with her and dies. The female then has no womb in which to bear her offspring in her belly; so when the young have grown in her belly, they tear open her side, and come forth, and kill her; they are therefore slayers of both father and mother.

div.head: Concerning the Serpent
div.p: The Lord said in the Gospel: "be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the serpent, that it has four natures.

Its first nature is this: when it grows old, it is hindered in its eyes, and if it wishes to become young, it disciplines itself and fasts forty days and forty nights, until its skin grows loose; and it seeks a rock or a narrow crack, and squeezing itself out from there, presses its body, and casting off its old age, becomes young again.

In this same manner, O man, if you wish to cast off the old age of the world, melt your body through fasting, by the narrow and constricted way; "for narrow and constricted is the way that leads to eternal life."
The second nature of the serpent: when the serpent comes to a spring to drink water, it does not carry its venom with it, but leaves it behind in its lair.

We too, then, ought, hastening to the ever-flowing and harmless water, full of divine and heavenly words, in the Church of God, not to carry with us the venom of wickedness, but to cast it away from ourselves entirely, and approach purely.
The third nature of the serpent: when the serpent sees a man naked, it is afraid and turns away; but when it sees him clothed, it leaps upon him.

[Well then has the Physiologus spoken.] Let us too understand spiritually that when our father Adam was naked in paradise, the devil was not able to fetter him. If, then, you too wear the garment of the old man, that is, the fig-leaves of pleasure, being grown old in evil days, it leaps upon you.
The fourth nature of the serpent: when a man comes upon it wishing to kill it, it gives up its whole body to death, guarding only its own head.

[Well then has the Physiologus said.] We too ought, in a time of temptation, to give up our whole body to death, guarding only our head, that is, not denying Christ, just as the holy martyrs did; "for the head of every man is Christ," as it is written.

div.head: Concerning the Ant
div.p: Solomon spoke in the Proverbs: "go to the ant, thou sluggard."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the ant, that it has three natures.

Its first nature is this: when they walk in a row, each one carries a grain in its mouth, and the empty ones, who have nothing, do not say to the laden ones, "give us of your grains," nor do they seize it by force, but go off and gather for themselves.
These sayings may be found applied to the wise virgins and the foolish.

[Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the ant.] The second nature of the ant: when it stores up grain in the earth, it cuts the grains in two, lest, when winter comes, the grains grow wet and sprout, and the ants starve. [And again the ant knows by its own wisdom whether there is to be heat, or whether the air is about to rain. When, then, you observe the ant carrying the grain of wheat from outside its hole in, know that a wintry air is coming; but if it carries its food from inside outward and spreads it out, know that there is calm weather.]

And the perfect ascetics hide the sayings of the old law from the letter, in the spirit, lest the letter kill you; for Paul said that "the Law is spiritual." For attending only to the bare letter, the Jews starved, and became murderers of saints.

The third nature of the ant: often the ant goes into the field at the time of harvest and climbs up the ear of corn, and brings down the grain, and before climbing up it, it smells at the stalk of the ear, and by the smell knows whether it is barley or wheat; and if it is barley, it does not climb up, but if it is wheat, it climbs up and brings the grain down. For barley is the food of beasts, as Job also says: "let barley come up for me instead of wheat."

Flee, then, you too, the food of beasts, and take the wheat that is stored up in the heavenly granary. For the barley is compared to the teaching of the heterodox, but the wheat to the most orthodox faith of Christ.

div.head: Concerning Sirens and Centaurs
div.p: Isaiah the prophet spoke, that "demons and sirens and hedgehogs shall dance in Babylon."
The Physiologus spoke concerning sirens and centaurs:

there are creatures in the sea called sirens, who sing tunefully with voices like the Muses, and those sailing past, if they hear their melody, cast themselves into the sea and perish. And the one half, down to the navel, has the shape of a human, but the other half, outward, that of a goose. In like manner the centaurs have the one half the shape of a man, but the other half, from the chest outward, that of a horse.

So too every double-minded man is unstable in all his ways. There are some who gather in the Church, having the outward form of piety but denying the power thereof, and in the Church they are as men, but when they are released from the Church, they turn into beasts. Such men, then, take on the persons of sirens and centaurs, I mean of the opposing powers and of mocking heretics; for by their smooth talk and fair speech, like the sirens, they deceive the hearts of the innocent. "For evil communications corrupt good manners." Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning sirens and centaurs.

div.head: Concerning Sirens and Centaurs (continued)
div.p: "Evil communications corrupt good manners," says the holy Apostle.
The Physiologus said that there are said to be certain creatures, male and female:

the male, down to the navel, is a man, but the rest a horse; likewise the female, down to the navel, resembles a woman, but the rest has the shape of a goose, and she is called a siren. "For the song of the sirens," says Job.

These, then, take on the persons of the opposing powers and of the godless and erring heretics. For there are, indeed there are, some full of hypocrisy, deceivers and cheats, who, creeping into the Church of God, deceive by their smooth talk the hearts of the innocent. But let us flee such men, not being deceived along with them by their false teachings; for just as these creatures are said to exist, though they do not, but are the fashioning of an evil imagination, so too is the deceptive false speech of deceivers and false Christs. For they have the outward form of piety, but have denied the power thereof.

div.head: Concerning the Hedgehog
div.p: Hedgehogs have the shape of a ball [and the likeness of a pig], and are wholly covered with spines. The Physiologus spoke concerning the hedgehog, that

it climbs, he says, upon the vine, and comes to the bunch of grapes, and knocks the berries down to the ground, and rolls itself among them, [and casts itself onto its back looking upward], and the berries stick fast to its spines, and it carries them off to its young, and leaves the branch of the bunch bare.

And so you too, O citizen, take your stand by the spiritual and true vine, that you may be brought into the spiritual winepress and stored up in the courts of the kingdom, and pass into the holy tribunal of Christ. For how have you let the hedgehog, the evil spirit, climb up upon your heart, and, after the manner of the bunch of grapes, leave you desolate, having in you no branch at all? [Rightly, then, as it has been said, has the Physiologus fitted to us the natures of the animals set down in the divinely inspired Scripture.]

div.head: Concerning the Fox
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning the fox, that it is a deceitful creature.

For if it hungers and finds no prey to eat, it seeks where it may find a muddy patch of ground or a chaff-heap, and casts itself down looking upward, and draws its breath into itself, and swells up entirely; and the birds, thinking that it is dead, settle down upon it to eat it, and so, rising up, it seizes them and devours them.

So too the devil is entirely deceitful, and so are his deeds; whoever wishes to partake of his flesh, dies. For these are his flesh: fornications, love of money, pleasures, murders. For this reason Herod too was likened to the fox, as also the scribe who heard from the Saviour: "the foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests." And in the Song of Songs Solomon says, "take us the little foxes, that spoil the vines." And David says in the Psalms, "they shall be a portion for foxes," and so forth. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the fox.

div.head: Concerning the Panther
div.p: The prophet prophesied and said, "I am become as a panther to Ephraim."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the panther, that it has such a nature as this: it is the friend of all creatures, but the enemy of the dragon alone; it is many-coloured, like Joseph's coat, and beautiful, and very gentle and mild.

If it eats and is satisfied, it sleeps in its lair, and on the third day it rises from sleep, and cries out with a great voice, and the beasts, both far and near, hear its voice; and from its voice comes forth every fragrance of spices, and the beasts, following the fragrance of the panther's voice, come very near to it.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead on the third day, cried out: "today is salvation to the world, both visible and invisible," and there came to be for us, both far and near, every fragrance, and peace, as the Apostle said. Many-coloured is the spiritual wisdom of God, as it is also said in the Psalm: "the queen stood at thy right hand, clothed in raiment of gold, in many colours," [which is the Church]. [Many-coloured is Christ, being himself virginity, continence, almsgiving, faith, virtue, concord, peace, patience; but he is also the enemy of the apostate dragon, that is in the water.] Nothing, then, as has been said, has the divine Scripture spoken idly concerning birds and beasts. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the panther.

div.head: Concerning the Aspidochelone
div.p: Solomon exhorts in the Proverbs, saying: "give no heed to a wicked woman; for honey drips from the lips of a harlot woman, who for a season makes smooth thy throat, but afterwards thou shalt find her more bitter than gall, and sharper than a two-edged sword. For the feet of folly lead down those who consort with her, after death, into Hades."

There is a sea-monster called the aspidochelone, having two natures. Its first nature is this: if it hungers, it opens its mouth, and every fragrance of spices comes forth from its mouth, and the little fish smell it, and gather together into its mouth, and it swallows them down; but the large and full-grown fish I do not find drawing near to the sea-monster.

So too the devil and the heretics, by their smooth talk and deceit, which seems to be fragrance, entice the childish and those imperfect in understanding; but the perfect in mind they cannot restrain, such as Job, a perfect fish, Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the whole choir of the prophets; as Judith escaped Holofernes, Esther Artaxerxes, Susanna the elders, Thecla Thamyris.

The other nature of the sea-monster: it is very great, like an island; and sailors, not knowing this, moor their ships to it as to an island, and fix the anchors and stakes of their ships, and kindle a fire upon the sea-monster to cook something for themselves; and when it grows warm, it sinks into the depth and drowns the ships.
And so you too, if you hang yourself upon the hope of the devil, he will sink you together with himself into the Gehenna of fire.
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the aspidochelone.

div.head: Concerning the Partridge
div.p: Jeremiah the prophet says: "the partridge called, she gathered what she did not hatch, making her wealth not with justice; in the midst of her days they shall leave her, and at her end she shall be a fool."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the partridge, that she broods and hatches the eggs of others; but when they are grown, each kind flies up to its own parents, and leaves her alone and foolish.

So too the devil seizes the race of infants in their minds; but when they come to the full measure of age, they begin to recognize their heavenly parents, that is, Christ and the Church and the holy prophets and apostles, and they leave him alone and foolish.
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the partridge.

div.head: Concerning the Vulture
div.p: Well did our Lord and Saviour say in the Gospel: "woe unto them that are with child, and to them that give suck, in those days."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the vulture, that it lodges in high and lofty places, and sleeps upon high rocks or upon the peaks of mountains. If it becomes pregnant, it travels to India and takes the birth-easing stone. This stone is round like a nut, and if you wish to move it, another stone shakes within it, like a bell striking and ringing; and if the vulture is overtaken by her travail, she sits upon the birth-easing stone and gives birth without pain.

And so you too, O man, having become pregnant with the Holy Spirit, take the spiritual birth-easing stone, rejected by the builders, who was made the head of the corner; and sitting upon him, as Isaiah the prophet said, may you bring forth the spirit of salvation: "for through fear of thee, O Lord, we have conceived, and travailed, and brought forth the spirit of thy salvation, which we have wrought upon the earth." For truly this stone that eases the birth of the Holy Spirit is our Lord Jesus Christ, cut out without hands, that is, born of a Virgin without the seed of man; and just as the birth-easing stone had another stone within it, ringing, so too the Lord's body had within it his Godhead, resounding.
Well then has the Physiologus said concerning the vulture.

div.head: Concerning the Ant-Lion
div.p: Eliphaz king of the Themanites said: "the ant-lion perished for lack of prey."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the ant-lion, that its fore parts are those of a lion, but its hind parts those of an ant. Its father is a flesh-eater, but its mother eats pulse; and when they beget the ant-lion, they beget it with two natures, and it is unable to eat flesh because of its mother's nature, nor pulse because of its father's nature; it perishes, therefore, for lack of food.

So too every double-minded man is unstable in all his ways. One ought not to walk two paths, nor speak two things in prayer; for woe, it is said, to the double heart, and to the sinner that walks upon two paths. It is not good to say yes and no, and no and yes, but yes, yes, and no, no, as our Lord Jesus Christ said.
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the ant-lion.

div.head: Concerning the Weasel
div.p: The Law says: "thou shalt not eat the weasel, nor that which is like it."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the weasel, that it has such a nature as this: it conceives by its mouth, from the male, and, being made pregnant, gives birth through its ears; wickedly, then, do they give birth by way of the hearing.

There are some who eat the spiritual bread in the Church; but when they go out, they cast the word out of their ears, resembling the unclean weasel, and become like a deaf asp that stops her ears. Eat not, then, the weasel, nor that which is like it.

div.head: Concerning the Unicorn
div.p: The Psalm says: "and my horn shall be exalted like the horn of the unicorn."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the unicorn, that it has such a nature as this: it is a small creature, like a kid, but exceedingly fierce; a hunter cannot come near it, because of its great strength, and it has one horn, in the middle of its head. How then is it hunted? A pure virgin [arrayed] is set before it, and it leaps into her bosom, and the virgin suckles the creature, and carries it off to the king's palace.

The creature, then, is applied to the person of the Saviour; "for he raised up a horn in the house of David his father," and became for us a horn of salvation. Angels and powers could not restrain him, but he tabernacled in the womb of the true and pure Virgin Mary [the Mother of God], "and the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us."

div.head: Concerning the Beaver
div.p: There is a creature called the beaver, exceedingly gentle and quiet, and its necessary parts are used for healing. When it is pursued by hunters, and knows that it is about to be caught, it bites off its own necessary parts, and casts them to the hunter; and if it should again fall in with another hunter and be pursued, the beaver throws itself on its back, and shows itself to him, and the hunter, understanding thereby that it has no more such parts, withdraws from it.

And so you too, O citizen, give the hunter his due. The hunter is the devil, and his due is fornication, adultery, murder; cut off such things and give them to the devil, and the hunting devil will let you be, that you too may say, "our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers."
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the beaver.

div.head: Concerning the Hyena
div.p: The Law says: "thou shalt not eat the hyena, nor that which is like it."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the hyena, that it is both male and female: sometimes it becomes male, sometimes female; it is a defiled beast, because it changes its own nature.

For this reason Jeremiah too says: "is my heritage unto me as the den of a hyena?" Be not you, then, likened to the hyena, embracing now the male, now the female nature, of whom, rebuking them, the holy Apostle spoke, saying: "men with men working unseemliness."
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the hyena.

div.head: Concerning the Otter
div.p: There is a creature called the otter, having the shape of a dog, and it is the enemy of the crocodile. As the crocodile sleeps, it has its mouth open; the otter, then, goes off, and smears its whole body with mud, and when the mud has dried, it leaps into the crocodile's mouth, and eats through all its passages, and devours its inward parts.

The crocodile, then, resembles the devil, but the otter is taken as the person of our Saviour; for our Lord Jesus Christ, taking on earthly flesh, went down into Hades, and loosed the pains of death, saying to those in bonds, "come forth," and to those in darkness, "be uncovered." And again the Apostle says, "O death, where is thy sting? O Hades, where is thy victory?" And he rose on the third day from the dead, raising up together with himself the earthly substance.

div.head: Concerning the Ichneumon
div.p: There is a creature called the ichneumon, [resembling a pig], the great enemy of the dragon. When it finds a wild dragon, as the Physiologus says, it goes and smears itself with mud, and guards its nostrils with its tail, until it has killed the dragon.

So too our Saviour took on the substance of earthly kind, until he killed the dragon Pharaoh, who sat upon the river of Egypt, that is, the devil. For if Christ were bodiless, how could he have destroyed the dragon? The dragon would have answered him, "thou art God and Saviour, and I have no power against thee." But he who is greater than all humbled himself, that he might save all.

div.head: Concerning the Crow
div.p: Well did Jeremiah say to Jerusalem: "thou hast sat as a desolate crow."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the crow, that it is monogamous, and when her husband dies, she no longer unites with another male, nor does the raven with another female.

The Synagogue of the Jews, the earthly Jerusalem, having murdered the Lord... for Christ no longer becomes her husband; "for I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to the Lord," but they committed adultery with wood and stone. If, then, we too keep the husband in our heart, the adulterer, the devil, does not enter in; but if the manly word departs from our soul, the adversary steals in; "for he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep," [and robbers no longer enter into your spiritual heart].
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the crow.

div.head: Concerning the Turtledove
div.p: In the Song of Songs Solomon bears witness and says: "the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the turtledove, that she is monogamous and exceedingly given to withdrawal, and dwells in desert places; she does not love to be in the midst of a crowd.

So too our Saviour lodged upon the Mount of Olives; for Jesus, taking Peter and James and John, [they went up] into the mountain, and Moses and Elijah appeared to them, and a voice came from heaven, saying, "this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; [hear ye him]." The turtledove loves to withdraw, and let the noblest Christ-bearers love to withdraw likewise. "For as a turtledove, so will I cry, and as a dove, so will I mourn." "The turtledove and the swallow, the sparrows of the field, knew the time of their coming." [So too you, O man.]
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the turtledove.

div.head: Concerning the Turtledove and the Dove
div.p: "As a turtledove, so will I cry, and as a dove, so will I mourn."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the turtledove, that she is exceedingly given to crying out; and when she is widowed, she dies together with the memory of him who has departed, and does not join with another.

The birds are to be likened to Christ; for he is our spiritual, most vocal turtledove, the truly sweet-voiced sparrow, who by his evangelical proclamations sang forth beneath heaven, to whom the bride herself, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, called out: "show me thy face, and let me hear thy voice, for thy voice is sweet, and thy face is comely." He himself is the gentle and truly guileless dove, having no deceit; for guile was not found in his mouth, according to what is written.
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the turtledove.

div.head: Concerning the Frog
div.p: There is a land-frog and a water-frog. The Physiologus spoke concerning the land-frog, that it endures the burning heat of the sun and the blazing fire; but when a violent winter overtakes it, it dies. But the water-frog, if it comes from the water and the sun touches it, at once dives back again into the water.

The noblest citizens resemble the land-frog; for they bear the burning heat of temptations; and if a violent winter overtakes them, that is, persecution for virtue's sake, they die. But those of the world are watery; for as soon as a little heat of temptation or desire touches them, unable to bear it, they dive back again into the same appetite of lust. Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the frog.

div.head: Concerning the Stag and the Serpent
div.p: David says: "as the hart longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for thee, O God."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the stag, that it is the great enemy of the dragon. If the dragon flees from the stag into the cracks of the earth, the stag goes and fills its vessels with spring water, and vomits it into the cracks of the earth, and draws the dragon out, and cuts it to pieces, and kills it.

So too our Lord killed the great dragon [the devil] with the heavenly waters, which he had, as it is said in the Theologian, of virtuous wisdom; for the dragon cannot bear water, nor the devil a heavenly word. The Lord, being present, drove out the great dragon [the devil, from the heavenly waters]; and the devil hid himself in the lower parts of the earth, as though hiding in a great crack, and the Lord, pouring out from his side blood and water, took away the dragon from us through the bath of regeneration, and took away every diabolical working hidden within us. [The stag is named from destroying serpents; "ophis" [serpent] being "ho phes," that is, he who once spoke to Eve.] If you too have understanding in your heart, call upon the Gospels, and they will say to you: "thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not fornicate, thou shalt not steal; having tasted of these spiritual waters, thou shalt vomit out all wickedness." And you too, O man, if you have spiritual dragons dwelling in your heart, call upon the Gospels, and they say to you: "thou shalt not murder, thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not bear false witness." If you hearken to the spiritual waters, you will vomit out all wickedness, and your heart becomes a temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. And so you too, O citizen, fill your vessels with the evangelical words of the Lord, and they will say to you: "thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not fornicate, thou shalt not murder, thou shalt not commit adultery," and keeping these, and casting away all wickedness, vomit it out, and you shall kill the dragon that is the origin of evil, that is, the devil. The ascetics, then, resemble the stag in another way also, those who lead a virtuous and toilsome life through much hardship, who, as though thirsting, run to the springs of saving repentance, and through the tears of confession quench the fiery darts of the evil one, and trampling upon the great dragon, that is, the devil, kill him. For if the hairs of a stag appear in a house, or if one burns its bone as incense, you shall never perceive the smell or the trace of a dragon; for wherever the fear of Christ is found in your heart, no evil drug ever rises up into your heart.
The Physiologus, then, has not spoken idly concerning the stag.

div.head: Concerning the Stag (continued)
div.p: The Physiologus said this also: the stags, wherever they come upon a serpent, swallow it down, and it runs and is driven on violently; and being driven and running, not stopping for two or three days, the serpent is dissolved within it; and when the beast has dissolved it, the stag urinates it out below through its urethra, and wherever that urine falls, there grows an unmixed shrub.
So too you, understanding man, having toiled and run much, shall be able to cast off the foul stench of the devil.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the stag.

div.head: Concerning the Salamander
div.p: There is a creature called the salamander. The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that if it enters a fiery furnace, the whole furnace is quenched, and if it enters the furnace-chamber of a bath-house, the furnace-chamber is quenched.

If then the salamander quenches fire by its own nature, how do some even now disbelieve that the three youths, cast into the furnace, suffered no harm, but instead cooled the furnace? For it is written, that even if thou walk through the fire, the flame shall not burn thee. [So too you, O man, may you be able to quench the eternal and unquenchable flame.] If then the salamander quenches fire by its own nature, how much more likely is it that the righteous, who walked according to righteousness, quenched the fire and stopped the mouths of lions?

div.head: Concerning the Three Holy Youths
div.p: It is a marvel, the story written in Daniel the prophet concerning the three most noble holy youths, who were cast into the fiery furnace through slander, and sang hymns [so as to be marvelled at]; for they happened to be righteous. And what marvel would there truly be, if the holy apostles too raised the dead, and did greater works than the righteous, and moved mountains in the sea?

div.head: Concerning the Three Holy Youths (continued)
div.p: A truly extraordinary marvel, and the mystery of the three most noble youths, who were cast into the fiery furnace, and who even raised the dead, as did their Master. For to quench so great a power of fire, and to master the disorder of that time and the tyranny of those in power and their own boldness, is a marvel truly worthy, and exceedingly fitting both for us and for those who meet with it, as most profitable. Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the salamander.

div.head: Concerning the Adamant Stone
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning the adamant stone, that it is found in the eastern region, and is not found by day, but by night; and it is called "adamas" because it masters all things, but is itself mastered by nothing.

And our Lord Jesus Christ judges all, but is himself judged by none; for he himself said, "which of you convicteth me of sin?" [It is found by night, not by day. Hear what he says:] "the people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and to them that sat in the region and shadow of death, light has sprung up." [It is found, then, in the east.] For truly, according to the prophet, "the Dayspring" is his name, and [again it is written elsewhere]: "there shall arise a star out of Jacob." And men too have become like the adamant, such as Job, a man from the risings of the sun, unable to be mastered by the evil one, and such as the apostles became, having loved the Dayspring, Christ, as Paul too somewhere says: "if ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me," beaten by the Jews, in prisons, in persecutions, in tumults, enduring perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils among false brethren; and just as the adamant did not yield, but endured nobly, and was not overcome by those who afflicted it, so too let the whole choir of the prophets and saints be understood. All the holy prophets and apostles, then, having the Dayspring as their adamant, did not yield under torments, but nobly enduring, were not overcome. The stone, then, is found in the night, not in the day. "For the people who sat in the region [of darkness] and the shadow of death, light has sprung up for them," for those who were once, long ago, the Jews, being children, and day did not rise for them, because it is said: "he came unto his own, and his own received him not," and light rose for us, who sat in darkness and the shadow of death. [And it is written in Amos the prophet, that I saw an adamant.] If you find yourself in the eastern regions, you are destined to be cast as righteous, blameless, God-fearing, like Job also, the noblest of those from the risings of the sun.
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the adamant stone, that it masters all things, but is itself mastered by nothing.
John said: "I saw the heavens opened, and the spirit of God descending upon him, and a voice out of the heavens saying: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; believe in him."

The exposition of the Physiologus: "a voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways smooth, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God." A heavenly and fatherly grace of our Lord Jesus Christ has overtaken us; receiving his commandments, we shall be saved.

div.head: How the Adamant Is to Be Understood
div.p: There is also a stone called adamant: it is not cut by iron, nor is it softened by engraving, nor is it even melted by all-devouring fire, but only by the blood of a goat, because this, though hotter than all else, is wont to soften the hardness and unyieldingness of the stone. This adamant, they say, is also found by night, and in the eastern region.

Why then, and for what reason, was such a paradoxical nature brought forth into this life? So that, when someone is found disbelieving the divine proclamation concerning Christ, he may be seen, though unwilling, to be unpersuaded, and may readily accept the mystery, looking to the adamant itself. For by night was the Master of all, Christ, found also, in the east, at Bethlehem, as one of us, as a man. And he is invincible in strength; for whatever kings, rulers and tyrants have plotted against him, they have all failed of their purpose; for as though assailing Christ the adamant, all were proven powerless. And that the adamant is indeed a clear prefiguring of Christ, hear also the prophet Amos saying: "behold, I set an adamant in the midst of my people Israel, and the altars of laughter shall be overthrown, and the rites of Israel shall be made desolate." Take heed, then, whether it was not by the very invincible strength of Christ himself that the altars of the idols were overthrown, and the rites of Israel became utterly desolate; and yet Christ, so great and unconquered in strength, being found greater than all, is bent, like the adamant, only by warm blood. And this is plain from what the Lord himself said to the sons of Zebedee, when they came to him seeking to sit on his right hand and on his left: "can ye drink of the cup that I drink of?" And the great Paul too plainly showed this very thing, saying thus: "ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin"; by warm blood, then, like the adamant, is even the unconquered Christ conquered, his own inward affections softened, and thereby he grants the kingdom in the heavens.

div.head: Concerning the Swallow
div.p: The swallow, when winter has passed, appears in spring, and sings at dawn, waking the sleepers to work.

And the perfect ascetics, when the winter of the body has passed, that is, when every fleshly desire has been quenched, then, being pure, remembering the Lord upon their beds, meditate upon him in the early mornings, rousing those weighed down by sleep to do good, and crying out: "awake, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light." [By "the dead" he means the Jews, over whom they sleep, not working good.]
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning [the season and] the swallow.

div.head: Concerning the Swallow (continued)
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning the swallow, that she gives birth once, and no longer bears again.
My Saviour was conceived once, born once, crucified once, buried once, and rose from the dead once. "One God, one faith, one baptism, one father of all."
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the swallow.

div.head: Concerning the Peridexion Tree
div.p: There is a tree in India called the peridexion, and its fruit is exceedingly sweet and most excellent. Doves delight greatly, being fed from the fruit of that tree (for they lodge upon it); and the dragon is at war and enmity with the dove. The dragon fears that tree and its shadow, in which the doves lodge, and the dragon cannot come near the dove, nor even near the shadow of the tree. If the shadow of the tree leans toward the west, the dragon flees to the east, and if it comes to the east, it flees to the west. If, then, the dove strays in the darkness away from the tree, the dragon, finding her, kills her.

The tree, then, is understood as the Father of all, as Gabriel said to Mary: "the Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." "For it is a tree of life to all who lay hold of it," "which shall yield its fruit in its season," and, "in the shadow of thy wings will we hope." And the shadow of holy Peter drove away destructive death from men. If, then, we too hold fast to wisdom and eat the fruits of the Spirit, which are joy, peace, self-control, patience, the wicked devil does not come near us; but if we stray among the things of darkness, which are fornication, adultery, idolatry, passions, evil desires and covetousness, the devil, finding us not abiding by the tree of life, easily destroys us. For this reason the Apostle too, knowing that the wood of the cross destroys the demon, cried out: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of the Lord, through whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world."

Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the peridexion tree. By the tree, beloved, understand the commandments of God, and as long as a man keeps them, he does not fear the devil; but when he despises the commandments of God, then the dragon overtakes him.

div.head: Concerning the Dove
div.p: John said, "I saw the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit descending as a dove out of heaven, and abiding upon him, and a voice came out of the heavens, saying: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

[The Physiologus spoke concerning many doves. For there are dove-keepers, and there are many kinds of doves, of many colours: the starling-grey, the black-hued, the golden-formed, the wholly white, the fiery-coloured.] The Physiologus spoke concerning the doves, that if the keeper sends out all the doves, none of them brings in or persuades any of the other keepers' doves to enter its own cote, except the fiery-coloured dove alone, which brings them all in and persuades them.

The Father sent forth beforehand, before the coming of Christ, as it were doves, to call all to life: Moses, Elijah, Samuel, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the rest of the prophets, and none was able to bring men in to life; but when our Lord Jesus Christ was sent forth from the heavens by the Father, by his own blood he brought all in to life, saying, "come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." [Rahab the harlot, believing in the sign of scarlet, was saved, her soul and her whole spiritual scarlet thread and her house. And in the Song of Songs Solomon says, "thy lips are like a scarlet thread." And Mary too took the scarlet and the true purple to work, being appointed by lot to do this. And it is written in the Gospel according to Matthew that the Lord, about to be crucified, was clothed in a scarlet cloak, but in the Gospel according to John, that he was clothed in purple, and this too is mystical: Matthew, through the scarlet, interpreted the dispensation according to the flesh, but John, through the purple, showed forth his kingship; for none wears purple, save the king alone.]
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the fiery-coloured dove.

div.head: Concerning the Same Doves
div.p: The Physiologus said that if all the doves fly together as one, the swift-winged hawk dares not come near any of them at all, on account of the harmonious sound of their wings; but if it finds one that has strayed, it easily seizes and devours her.

This is applied to the order of virgins: that if they gather together in the Church as a flock, sending up a tuneful hymn through prayers and psalms in concord to God, their adversary the devil dares not come near any of them at all, fearing their great prayer and psalmody; but if he finds one that has strayed, he easily seizes and kills her. Let none, then, forsake the gathering together unto God, not the virgin alone, but every Christian, lest he become the prey of the evil one.

div.head: Concerning the Dove (continued)
div.p: The Lord again said, "and harmless as doves."
For those birds, being robbed of their young, bear no grudge against those who do this, but devise another nest, that, nesting there, they may again provide themselves with other young.
So too he prepares us to be harmless toward all, and, being robbed, not to bear a grudge nor to retaliate, but with joy to accept all things that come upon us.

div.head: Concerning the Creature Hydrus
div.p: There is a creature called the hydrus, exceedingly fierce, so that no hunter is able to come near it [because of its great strength]; it has long horns [upon its head], shaped like a saw, so that it saws through great and lofty trees and brings them down to the ground. If it thirsts, it comes to the river Euphrates, and drinks; and there are slender-branched heath-shrubs there, and the creature begins to play against the heath [among its branches] with its horns, and, becoming entangled, is held fast to the branches of the heath, and cries out, wishing to escape, and cannot, [for it is entangled]. The hunter, then, hearing it crying out [and understanding that it is held fast], comes and slaughters the creature.

And so you too, O citizen, having two horns, the Old and the New Testament, with which you may gore your enemies -- fornication, adultery, love of money, arrogance, and all the passions of matter -- do not become entangled with them, which hold you fast after the manner of the heath, lest the evil hunter destroy you.

div.head: Concerning the Fire-Striking Stones
div.p: There are stones which, when they draw near to one another, kindle and set fire to everything that falls upon them; and there is such a nature to them, male and female, but they stand far apart from one another.

And so you too, most noble citizen, flee the female, lest, drawing near to her, you be kindled unto pleasure, and burn up all the virtue that is in you. For Samson too, drawing near to a woman, was shorn of his strength, and many, according to what is written, have been led astray by the beauty of women.

div.head: Concerning the Fire-Striking Stones (continued)
div.p: There are fire-striking stones in the eastern region, male and female; as long as they are far from one another, fire burns nowhere, but if the male draws near to the female, fire is kindled and sets everything ablaze.

O most noble citizen, angels are in gloom and Tartarus on account of women. Samson and Solomon and Joseph, righteous men, fell into snares, and many, according to what is written, have been led astray by the beauty [and comeliness] of woman.

div.head: Concerning the Magnet Stone
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning the magnet stone, that it draws up iron; [having attached the iron to the stone, it draws it up].
If, then, created things draw one another up, how much more the Creator and Maker of all [God], who hung up the heaven from the earth and stretched it out like a curtain?
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the magnet stone.

div.head: Concerning the Sea-Creature Called the Saw
div.p: There is a creature in the sea called the saw, having long wings, and if it sees ships sailing under sail, it too imitates them, and raises its wings, and sails, competing with the sailing ships; but if it goes on for thirty or forty stades, it grows weary, and draws its wings in to itself [wearied], and the waves carry it back to its old place.

The sea, then, is taken as the world, and the ships as the persons of the apostles and martyrs, who, crossing over as it were a sea, buffeted by the waves, that is, by the affairs of life [and its billows], reached a calm harbour, the kingdom of the heavens; but this creature is likened to those who begin the life of asceticism, and then turn back to their former manner of life in the world, [just as this creature also, unable to sail on with the ships, was left behind].

Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the saw. Understand the sea as the world, the ships as the holy apostles, who crossed over this age and the opposing powers; but the saw, which did not endure to sail on with the ships, is applied to those who lived rightly only for a time, and did not endure to the end. For having begun good works, they did not endure to the end, on account of love of money, or arrogance, or adultery, or base gain, or fornication, or hatred, and the waves of the sea, that is, the opposing powers, carry them down into Hades. And just as the saw imitates the ships, so too do men who follow after virtue in order to cross out of this briny life -- for this is the sea -- and then, being deceived and not enduring to the end, that is, because of evil deeds, that is, the waves of the sea, are carried back down again into eternal torments. "For he that endureth to the end," it is said, "shall be saved."

div.head: Concerning the Ibis
div.p: The ibis is unclean according to the Law. It does not know how to swim, but grazes along the banks of rivers and pools, and cannot enter into the depths, where the clean fish swim, but only where the unclean little fish dwell.

Learn, then, you too, to swim spiritually, that you may come to the deep spiritual river, into the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God. For unless you stretch out your two hands and make the sign of the cross, you will not be able to cross the sea of life. For the figure of the cross extends over all created things: the sun, unless it stretches out its rays, cannot shine; the moon, unless it stretches out its two horns, does not shine; a bird, unless it stretches out its wings, does not fly. Moses, stretching out his hands, destroyed Amalek; Daniel, the lions. Jonah was cast into the belly of the whale, Thecla into fire and beasts and seals, and the figure of the cross preserved her. Susanna was saved from the elders, Judith from Holofernes, and Esther from Artaxerxes, and the three youths in the fiery furnace were saved [through faith], and worse than all of these is the ibis... [the offspring of sinners are sins].

div.head: Concerning the Gazelle
div.p: There is a creature [in the mountain] called the gazelle. The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that it greatly loves the high mountains, but finds its food on the level ground of the mountains, and it watches from afar all who approach it, and knows whether they come with deceit, or with friendship.

It is, then, a figure of the wisdom of God. This is she who loves [the prophets, that is,] the high mountains, as it is said: "behold, my beloved leaps upon the mountains, bounding upon the hills." [The mountains are taken for the prophets, the hills for the apostles.] Since, then, the gazelle is sharp-sighted, it signifies that the Saviour sees all that is done (for he is called God because he beholds our works), and knows those who come to him from afar with deceit, as he knew Judas, who betrayed him with a kiss. David too said, "the Lord knoweth them that are his," and John said, "behold the Lamb of God, that taketh away the sin of the world."

div.head: Concerning the Strong Adamant Stone
div.p: There is another nature of the [strong] adamant stone: it fears neither iron when struck, nor fire when burning, nor does it take on the smell of smoke. If it is found in a house, no demon enters there, nor is any evil found; and the man who holds it conquers every diabolical working.
The adamant is our Lord Jesus Christ; if, then, O man, you have him in your heart, no evil shall ever befall you.

div.head: Concerning the Elephant
div.p: There is a creature in the mountain called the elephant, [and another, the gergelephas]. In this creature there is no desire for intercourse; if, then, it wishes to beget offspring, it goes to the east, near paradise. There is a tree there called the mandrake; the female and the male go there, and the female, partaking first of the tree, gives also to her male and plays with him, until he too partakes; and the male, having eaten, unites with the female [from behind, because they have no joint for it; she carries the burden in her womb for one year], and she conceives at once. When the time comes for her to give birth, she goes to a pool of water [and enters into it], until the water comes up to her udders, and so she brings forth her offspring upon the water, and it comes to her thighs, and suckles at its mother's udder. The elephant guards her in her travail because of the serpent, since the serpent is the enemy of the elephant, and if the elephant finds it, it tramples and kills it. Now the nature of the elephant is this: if it falls, it cannot rise up again, for it has no joints in its knees [as the other creatures do]. And how does it fall? If it wishes to sleep, it leans itself against a tree and sleeps; the hunters, then, knowing the elephant's nature, go and saw the tree nearly through. Then the elephant comes to lean upon it, and falls together with the tree, and begins to cry out weeping, and another elephant hears, and comes to help it, and cannot raise it up; and the two cry out, and twelve elephants come, and not even they are able to raise up the fallen one; then all of them cry out; and last of all a small elephant comes, and puts its trunk beneath the fallen elephant, and raises it up. [Now the nature of the small elephant is this: if you burn its hairs or its bones as incense in any place, no demon, nor dragon, nor any evil thing enters there.]

The elephant and its mate, then, are taken as the persons of Adam and Eve; when they were in the delight of paradise before the transgression, they knew no intercourse then, nor had they any notion of union. But when the woman ate of the tree, that is, of the spiritual mandrakes, and gave also to her husband, then Adam knew his wife, and begot Cain upon the waters of blame, as David said: "save me, O God, for the waters are come in even unto my soul." Then came the great elephant, that is, the Law, and was not able to raise him up; then came the twelve elephants, that is, the choir of the prophets, and not even they were able to raise up the fallen one; but last of all came the spiritual and holy elephant [our Lord Jesus Christ], and raised man up from the earth. He who is greater than all [that is, Christ, the new Adam] became the servant of all; for he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, [becoming like unto them], that he might save all.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the elephant.

div.head: Concerning the Agate and the Pearl
div.p: When craftsmen seek the pearl, they find it by means of the agate. For they bind the agate with a strong cord, and let it down into the sea; and the agate goes to the pearl, and stands there, and is not moved, and at once the divers perceive the place of the agate, and following the cord, find the pearl. And how is the pearl formed? Listen: there is a shellfish in the sea called the oyster, and it rises up from the sea in the early hours of dawn, and the shell, opening its mouth and swallowing the heavenly dew and the ray of the sun and of the moon and of the stars, forms the pearl out of the lights above. The shell has two wings, wherein the pearl is found.

The agate, then, is understood as John; for he showed us the spiritual pearl, saying, "behold the Lamb of God, that taketh away the sin of the world." The sea, then, is taken for the world, and the divers for the choir of the prophets; and the two wings of the shell for the Old and the New Testament. Likewise the sun and the moon and the stars and the dew are for the Holy Spirit, who visits the two Testaments, and the pearl for our Saviour Jesus Christ [for he is the precious pearl], whom a man, finding, and selling all that he has [and giving to the poor], obtains the precious pearl.

div.head: Concerning Pearls
div.p: In India there was the present pinna, a shellfish, planted at the bottom of the sea, in want of fresh waters; in the month of Daimaios it brings water in India, and the pinna, being in need of fresh water, comes up out of the sea, and there is thunder, and lightning, and rain, and the pinna receives the roar of the thunder and the flashing fire of the lightning and the drop of the water, and then straightway goes back again to its own place. And the pinna, caught by men, they dig out the pearl, and, given to the goldsmith, who pierces it -- which nature does it undergo, that of the thunder, the lightning, or of the shell?

This, then, is applied to the dispensation of the Godhead made flesh. Through the thunder was the voice of the angel; through the lightning was the Godhead; through the water was the Word; and through the shell-covering was the Mother of God, that is, the purple of the shellfish, which dyed itself with her own blood for the King of hosts. Pierced, then, it is the nature of the shell-covering that suffers, that is, the flesh of mankind; for the Godhead remained impassible, as John of Damascus says, "the pearl, having conceived Christ from the divine lightning," and so forth. Let the Armenians and the Theopaschites be ashamed, who say, "God was crucified." And these, then, are the matters concerning the shellfish of the sea.

div.head: Concerning Pearls (continued)
div.p: In that same Red Sea the pearl is formed in abundance; and it comes about thus: in that sea there are shellfish called pinnae; these pinnae stand toward the shore, each one of them having its mouth open, that something may enter for its food. As it stands there gaping with its mouth, and as flashes of lightning come frequently, the power of the lightning is received within the pinna, and the pinna, taking fright, closes itself up; and the pinna having been closed, holding the lightning within, the lightning coils itself together with the little globes of the pinna's eyes, and, coiling, forms the two eyes into pearls. And so the pinna, crying out and dissolving, the pearls shine forth toward the Red Sea, and men, seeing them, go in and take them, and thus are pearls formed.

And just as the pearls are formed there in this manner, in the same way the most pure Mary, being cleansed from every defilement -- for the divine lightning came from heaven, the Son and Word of God, to be contained within the all-pure pinna, the Mother of God Mary, and from her was formed a pearl beyond price, concerning whom it is written: "having conceived Christ, the pearl of the divine lightning" -- and wise is the merchant who gives up all that he has, and buys the true pearl, Christ himself.

div.head: Concerning the Wild Ass and the Ape
div.p: There is another nature of the wild ass. The Physiologus said that it is found in royal courts, and on the twenty-fifth of the month of Phamenoth they know, from the wild ass, that the equinox has come; for if it brays twelve times, the king and the palace know that the equinox has come. In like manner also the ape, if it urinates seven times in the night, they know that the equinox has come.

The wild ass, then, is the devil, since the night, that is, the people of the Gentiles, has become equal to the day, that is, to the prophets who believed. [The wild ass, then, that is, the devil, cried out.] And the ape too takes on the person of that same devil; for it has a beginning, but no good end, that is, no tail, [just as the ape too has no good end, that is, no tail], as the devil too, [having no good end], was in the beginning one of the archangels, but his end was not found [good, just as the ape without a tail is not comely; for it is a deformity in the ape to have no tail].
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the wild ass and the ape.

div.head: Concerning the Indian Stone
div.p: There is an Indian stone, [called the frog-stone], having such a nature as this: if a man happens to be dropsical, the skilled physicians seek out that stone, and bind it upon the dropsical man for three hours, and the stone drinks up all the waters of the dropsical man. Then they loose the stone, and weigh it together with the man on the scale, and the small stone draws the man's body down on the scale. And if the stone is left in the sun for three hours, it pours out again all the corrupt waters which it took from the man's body, and the stone becomes clean again, as it was before.

The stone is our Lord Jesus Christ, the perfect love that casts out fear. Since we were dropsical, having the waters of the devil in our heart, the Lord came down and, bound through the cross to our hearts, healed our floods; for he himself took up our infirmities, and bore our sicknesses.
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the Indian stone.

div.head: Concerning the Bird Heron
div.p: The Psalmist said: "the dwelling of the heron is chief among them." The Physiologus said: this bird is exceedingly wise beyond many birds. It has one dwelling and one fold, and does not seek many resting-places, but wherever it settles, there it feeds and sleeps; nor does it eat a dead body, nor does it fly to many places; its resting-place and its food are in one place.

And so you too, O man leading a life in the world, do not seek the many places of the heretics; let there be for you one resting-place, the holy Church of God, and one food, the bread that came down from heaven, our Lord Jesus Christ; touch not dead teachings, that the heavenly bread may be plainly seen by you, and seek not the many places of the heterodox.
Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the bird heron.

div.head: Concerning the Sycamore
div.p: The blessed Amos says: "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son, but I was a herdsman, tending sycamore fruit." The herdsman tends goats; well then does Amos take on the person of Christ. And the saying "tending sycamore fruit" is a spiritual word; and Zacchaeus climbed up into a sycamore tree. You know that before the sycamore fruit is pricked, there are gnats within it, called mosquitoes, dwelling in darkness, seeing no light. They say among themselves, "what a great country we dwell in," while they sit in darkness. But when the sycamore fruit is pricked and they come out, they see the brightness of the sun and the moon and the stars, and say among themselves, "we were sitting in darkness [and the shadow of death] before the sycamore fruit was pricked." It is pricked, then, on the first day, and on the third day it is presented, and becomes food for all.

So the side of our Lord Jesus Christ was pierced by the lance, and there came out blood and water, and on the third day, when he rose from the dead, we saw the spiritual luminaries, just as the gnats, when the sycamore fruit was pricked, saw the undying luminaries. [The kids, then, take on the person of repentance, because from their hair a mourning garment is woven; "in sackcloth and ashes," it says, "they repented."] "The people that sat in darkness saw a great light, and to them that sat in the region and shadow of death light has sprung up." When the sycamore fruit is pricked, on the third day it becomes food; so too our Lord Jesus Christ, his side having been pierced, rose on the third day from the dead, and became life and food for us all.
